newsitem.title: UK: Mark soars against the lira after EMU comments.
newsitem.headline: Mark soars against the lira after EMU comments.

text.p: The mark climbed some nine lire on Tuesday and was holding near peaks in late Europe after a senior German government official said some EMU aspirants would be well advised to delay entry into the single currency.
State secretary to the German Finance Ministry Juergen Stark said some qualifiers should forsake the political prestige of joining economic and monetary union (EMU) at the outset.
There are some members whose economic structures are not yet well enough prepared to take part," he said.
While Stark did not name names, analysts said his comments appeared directed at countries like Italy or Spain.

Even some countries which qualify on paper "would be well advised to maintain exchange rate flexibility for a certain period, and...respect that they should not have to follow the rigid rules of the European Central Bank from the start," Stark said.

The mark shot up almost nine lire to a session peaks of 981.60 lire on the back of the comments. Traders said market talk the lira was overvalued against the mark also weighed on the Italian currency. The Mark/lira's central parity rate in the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) is 990.
The mark shaved some of its gains later after Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi said the lira exchange rate was sensible.
Traders said the lira was particularly sensitive to the comments because nervous speculators long of lira needed an excuse to pile out.
Don Smith, international economist at HSBC Markets, said in this atmosphere, investors would react to anything which fuels speculation about whether Italy will make it into the first round of EMU.
While the mark also appreciated against the peseta, the move was not as marked. Against the peseta, the mark stood at 84.37/4.40 at 1710 GMT against 84.16/4.18 in late Europe on Monday.

Keld Holm, international economist at Lehman Brothers, said the core-European countries, such as the Germany, France and the Benelux countries and Austria, have a stronger correlation and a more similar structure.
"For countries such as the UK or Italy and Spain, which have quite a different economic structure, it probably would make sense to stay out of orbit a little bit longer."
But, he said, this would not please countries in question which are working to meet EMU criteria.
But there is no doubt, said Holm, that the Germans want a solid foundation for the euro.

"The smaller group of countries you start with the more likely it (euro) will be solid and the more likely it will succeed. From an economic perspective that makes sense. But then there is the political agenda," he added.
